newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Metal trade doubtful on Russia Norilsk strike call.
newsitem.headline: Metal trade doubtful on Russia Norilsk strike call.

text.p: Western metals traders and analysts were sceptical on Tuesday that a strike threat by workers at Russia's troubled Norilsk Nickel group would lead to serious supply disruptions.
But they were not entirely discounting the possibility of some kind of action affecting output at one of the world's biggest producers of nickel and precious metals.
Benchmark three-month nickel futures on the London Metal Exchange (LME) rose to a 10-month high of $8,325 on Tuesday, up sharply from a December 1996 low of $6,365.

While the threat of major supply disruptions was remote, the fact that Norilsk's flagship plant produced 100,000 tonnes of nickel in 1996, or 10 percent of total world output, was deterring traders from selling, some analysts said.
"If there is no major strike, $500 (a tonne) will be knocked off the price," Jim Lennon, metals analyst at Macquarie Equities in London, said.
A Norilsk trade union spokesman said workers at the group's flagship plant would stage a one-hour warning strike on March 27 over salary and holiday arrears, with bigger action on April 2.
But the news left many nickel specialists cold.
"This is just a lot of posturing by the union to strengthen their bargaining position with management," said a senior London-based physical nickel trader.

Disruptions to nickel, cobalt, copper and platinum group metal exports would only deprive the company of much-needed hard currency earnings to pay off its huge arrears to workers, Angus MacMillan, analyst at Billiton Metals, said.
"I'd be very surprised if the union called an all-out strike. It would be a case of cutting off its nose to spite its face," he said.
But he added: "No one is going to go short of nickel while this strike threat rumbles on."
Neither were others discounting entirely the possibility of a surprise.
"There is still a good possbility that this could turn into a major dispute and send prices higher," a second European nickel trader said.

The Norilsk union spokesman said the scale of any strike would be decided by a committee but that it would involve suspending production in some way. He said 60 units making up the main plant would each decide how to disrupt output.
But a source at one of the Norilsk head plant's biggest units, the Nadezhdinsky metallurgical plant, said he did not think Nadezhdinsky workers would join any strike.
Analysts took this as a sign that the union, which says it represents most of the 120,000 workers at the main plant, known as the mining and metallurgical complex, might not have sufficient clout.
"This is significant, because it shows there is not a united stand at Norilsk," said Lennon.
Traders and analysts said management might be able to speed up arrears payments, because nickel prices on world markets are high and pre-financing credits from western banks are being released.

The Norilsk group owes workers 900 billion roubles ($160 million) in unpaid salaries and holidays and 1.2 trillion roubles ($211 million) to various budgets. It has a plan to pay worker arrears by the end of the year but unions want the money faster.
"The first tranche of the ABN Amro credit could improve the company's cash flow, as could the higher price of nickel," Lennon said.

Norilsk said on Monday that trading firm Interrosimpex, which handles Norilsk exports, had received the first $50 million tranche of a $200 million credit deal with ABN Amro (Moscow) Ltd to pre-finance supplies for export.

Lennon estimated that, based on the group's total nickel output of 177,185 tonnes in 1996, every 10-cent-per-pound ($220/tonne) rise in world prices would add nearly $40 million to Norilsk Nickel's annual cash flow.
